pattern_types.name: Softening disagreement to protect belonging
pattern_types.definition: When disagreement arises with someone whose approval matters, the person suppresses, delays or dilutes their own position. The driver is fear that conflict will damage the relationship, not lack of opinion.
frameworks: Young's subjugation and approval-seeking schema themes

signs.text: Apologises or hedges before stating a need
Reports agreeing in the moment, then resenting it later
Rehearses conversations to avoid upsetting someone
Describes the other's anger as the worst outcome, above the issue itself
Uses "it's fine" or "not a big deal" about something they then dwell on

signs_against.text: States disagreement directly with close others and reports little distress
Avoids conflict only with people who hold power over them (points to a situational or status driver)

look_alikes.name: Performance-contingent self-worth
look_alikes.tells_apart: Keeps quiet to protect the relationship; the other fears criticism as a verdict on their competence

look_alikes.name: Control-seeking under uncertainty
look_alikes.tells_apart: Keeps quiet because closeness is at stake; the other is uneasy about any unknown outcome, closeness or not

look_alikes.name: Saying yes and over-giving to feel needed
look_alikes.tells_apart: Says yes to avoid the friction of saying no; the other says yes to be needed and keep a place

look_alikes.name: Taking on other people's moods as theirs to fix
look_alikes.tells_apart: Stays quiet about their own view; the other acts to fix the other's mood

pattern_types.anyone_would: Keeping quiet over small things with strangers or people in charge

exclusions.text: Active relationship crisis
Grief

pattern_types.approved_wording: You seem to protect closeness by keeping disagreements small, even when they matter to you.
prediction_wordings: Next time {person} asks for something you'd rather not do, notice whether you say yes before you've decided.
Next time you go along with {person} on something, notice how you feel about it a few hours later.
Next time you disagree with someone you're not close to, like {person}, notice whether saying so feels any easier.

pattern_types.name: Pushing back at once when criticised
pattern_types.definition: When someone points out a fault or questions what the person did, they answer straight away with a counter-attack or a long explanation. The criticism lands as a threat to how they see themselves, so it has to be dealt with now, before it can be weighed.
pattern_types.if_situation: Criticised or told they got something wrong
pattern_types.then_behaviour: Hits back or explains themselves at once
pattern_types.function: To protect how they see themselves

signs.text: Replies to a complaint with a complaint of their own about the other person
Gives a long account of why it wasn't their fault before taking in what was said
Describes a small remark as an attack on who they are
Replays the criticism later, building the case they wish they'd made
Says feedback "came out of nowhere" when the other person had raised it before

signs_against.text: Asks what the other person meant, or agrees with part of it, before answering
Pushes back only when the criticism is clearly unfair and says why calmly

look_alikes.name: Performance-contingent self-worth
look_alikes.tells_apart: Turns the criticism outward and answers back; the other turns it inward and judges themselves

look_alikes.name: Going quiet and pulling away when hurt
look_alikes.tells_apart: Moves toward the other person to answer back; the other goes quiet and moves away

pattern_types.anyone_would: Standing up for themselves when someone is openly hostile or insulting

exclusions.text: The criticism came during a formal complaint, dismissal or legal dispute
Grief

pattern_types.approved_wording: When someone finds fault with you, you seem to answer it straight away, before you've had a chance to weigh whether any of it is fair.
prediction_wordings: Next time {person} points out something you did, notice what you say in the first few seconds, and whether it's an answer or a question.
Next time {person} points out something you did, notice what you think about it an hour later, once it has cooled.
Next time you spot a mistake of your own before anyone else does, notice how you talk to yourself about it.

pattern_types.name: Going quiet and pulling away when hurt
pattern_types.definition: When someone close hurts or lets them down, the person goes quiet, keeps to themselves and waits for it to pass rather than saying they were hurt. Showing the hurt would mean showing they need the other person, and that feels riskier than the distance.
pattern_types.if_situation: Hurt or let down by someone close
pattern_types.then_behaviour: Goes quiet, pulls away and doesn't say why
pattern_types.function: To avoid showing they need someone
frameworks: Attachment theory, the self-reliant end (Bowlby; Bartholomew)

signs.text: Stops replying or answers in short, flat messages after being hurt
Says "I'm fine" to the person who hurt them while clearly not fine
Expects the other person to notice and come to them without being told
Feels that saying "that hurt" would make them look weak or needy
Makes plans that keep them out of the person's way for a few days

signs_against.text: Tells the person soon after that something they did hurt
Takes some time alone to calm down, then comes back to talk it through

look_alikes.name: Pushing back at once when criticised
look_alikes.tells_apart: Goes quiet and moves away after a hurt; the other answers back at once and moves toward the fight

look_alikes.name: Pulling back when someone gets closer or needs more
look_alikes.tells_apart: Pulls away after being hurt; the other pulls away when things get close, with no hurt before it

look_alikes.name: Saying "I'm fine" and hiding what's hard
look_alikes.tells_apart: Hides a hurt from the one who caused it; the other hides any struggle from everyone so as not to weigh on them

pattern_types.anyone_would: Keeping distance from a stranger or acquaintance who was rude

exclusions.text: The person who hurt them is someone they need to be safe from
Grief
Active relationship crisis, such as a breakup in the last month

pattern_types.approved_wording: When someone close hurts you, you seem to go quiet and keep your distance rather than let them see it landed.
prediction_wordings: Next time {person} lets you down, notice whether you tell them, or wait for them to work it out.
Next time you go quiet on {person}, notice what you're hoping they will do.
Next time someone you're not close to lets you down, like {person}, notice whether it's easier to say so.

pattern_types.name: Asking others to confirm a choice already made
pattern_types.definition: After making a choice, the person asks one or more others whether it was right. They are not looking for new information; the choice is made. The asking quiets the fear of having got it wrong, until the next doubt.
pattern_types.if_situation: Has just made a choice that matters to them
pattern_types.then_behaviour: Asks others to confirm it was the right one
pattern_types.function: To quiet the fear of having got it wrong

signs.text: Asks several people the same "did I do the right thing?" about one choice
Feels relief when someone agrees, which fades within a day
Shares a decision as a question ("I've booked it, is that okay?")
Re-reads reviews or advice about something already bought or decided
Says they don't trust their own judgement on everyday things

signs_against.text: Makes a choice and moves on without checking it with anyone
Asks for others' views before deciding, then decides and stops asking

look_alikes.name: Reading silence as something wrong and reaching out to check
look_alikes.tells_apart: Checks whether they chose right; the other checks whether the bond is still okay

look_alikes.name: Control-seeking under uncertainty
look_alikes.tells_apart: Seeks agreement about a choice already made; the other seeks information or control over an outcome still open

look_alikes.name: Keeping options open and putting off committing
look_alikes.tells_apart: Commits, then looks for reassurance; the other doesn't commit at all

pattern_types.anyone_would: Checking a work decision with a manager who has to sign it off

exclusions.text: A big life decision in the last two weeks, such as a move or a new job
Grief

pattern_types.approved_wording: Once you've chosen, you seem to need someone else to say it was right before you can settle.
prediction_wordings: After your next {decision}, notice whether you ask anyone if it was right, and how long the relief lasts if they say yes.
Next time you decide something small, like {decision}, notice whether you can leave it alone without telling anyone.
Next time someone doubts a choice you've made about {decision}, notice what happens to how sure you felt a minute before.

pattern_types.name: Saying yes and over-giving to feel needed
pattern_types.definition: When someone asks for help, the person says yes and then gives more than was asked, often at a cost to themselves. Being the one others rely on is part of how they know they matter, so saying no feels like losing a place.
pattern_types.if_situation: Asked for help or a favour
pattern_types.then_behaviour: Says yes and gives more than was asked

signs.text: Agrees to help before checking whether they have the time
Turns a small favour into a much bigger job without being asked
Feels flat or useless on days nobody needs anything from them
Feels hurt when their help is turned down or not noticed
Describes themselves as "the one everyone calls"

signs_against.text: Says no to a request without much guilt and feels fine after
Helps a lot, but only where they chose to and it costs them little

look_alikes.name: Softening disagreement to protect belonging
look_alikes.tells_apart: Says yes to be needed and keep a place; the other says yes to avoid the friction of saying no

look_alikes.name: Taking on other people's moods as theirs to fix
look_alikes.tells_apart: Gives when asked; the other steps in to fix a mood without being asked

look_alikes.name: Doing it all themselves rather than leaning on others
look_alikes.tells_apart: Takes on other people's tasks to be needed; the other keeps their own tasks so as not to depend on anyone

pattern_types.anyone_would: Saying yes to a reasonable request from a manager at work

exclusions.text: Caring for a seriously ill or dependent family member
Grief

pattern_types.approved_wording: Being the one people turn to seems to matter a lot to you, so yes comes easily, even when it costs you.
prediction_wordings: Next time {person} asks you for something, notice whether you say yes before you've checked what it will cost you.
Next time you help {person}, notice whether you do more than they asked for, and how you feel if they don't mention it.
Next time {person} sorts something out without asking you, notice what you feel first.

pattern_types.name: Saying "I'm fine" and hiding what's hard
pattern_types.definition: When something is hard, the person keeps it to themselves and tells others they are fine. They worry that sharing it would weigh on people or make them less welcome, so they carry it alone and show an easy face.
pattern_types.if_situation: Going through something hard while others are around
pattern_types.then_behaviour: Says they're fine and keeps it to themselves

signs.text: Tells people they're fine during a week they describe as hard
Says they don't want to "dump" their problems on anyone
Turns a question about how they are into a question about the other person
Mentions something hard only after it's over, as a passing remark
Apologises for "going on" after sharing a little

signs_against.text: Tells a friend or family member when they're struggling and asks for support
Keeps something private by choice and feels at ease with that, not lonely

look_alikes.name: Going quiet and pulling away when hurt
look_alikes.tells_apart: Hides any struggle from everyone so as not to weigh on them; the other hides a hurt from the one who caused it

look_alikes.name: Doing it all themselves rather than leaning on others
look_alikes.tells_apart: Keeps their troubles to themselves so as not to be a weight; the other keeps their tasks to themselves so as not to be let down

pattern_types.anyone_would: Saying "fine, thanks" to a stranger or acquaintance who asks in passing

exclusions.text: Any sign the hard thing puts them at risk; that is for the Safeguard, never a Pattern
Grief
Serious illness, their own or a close family member's

pattern_types.approved_wording: When things are hard, you seem to keep them to yourself so you don't weigh on the people around you.
prediction_wordings: Next time someone asks how you are on a hard day, notice what you say, and what you'd have said if you weren't worried about weighing on them.
Next time {person} offers to help or to listen, notice what you say first, and whether you change the subject.
Next time something small goes wrong, like {thing}, notice whether you tell anyone, and who.

pattern_types.name: Keeping options open and putting off committing
pattern_types.definition: When a choice would close off other options, the person puts it off, keeps several open or commits only loosely. Being tied down feels like losing freedom, so not choosing feels safer, even when waiting costs them.
pattern_types.if_situation: A commitment would close off other options
pattern_types.then_behaviour: Delays deciding and keeps options open
frameworks: Self-determination theory, autonomy need (Deci and Ryan)

signs.text: Answers an invitation with "maybe" and decides on the day
Feels trapped or restless once something is fixed in the diary
Keeps two or more options going long past the point of choosing
Pays a cost, such as a higher price or a lost place, rather than commit early
Describes long-term plans as a cage

signs_against.text: Commits early to a plan and feels settled, not trapped
Delays only when they truly lack the information to choose

look_alikes.name: Asking others to confirm a choice already made
look_alikes.tells_apart: Doesn't commit at all; the other commits, then looks for reassurance

look_alikes.name: Pulling back when someone gets closer or needs more
look_alikes.tells_apart: Protects freedom around choices and plans; the other protects room from a person getting closer

pattern_types.anyone_would: Waiting to decide while an important fact is still unknown

exclusions.text: A choice forced by money trouble, illness or a visa

pattern_types.approved_wording: You seem to keep your options open for as long as you can, as if choosing one would take something away from you.
prediction_wordings: Next time you're asked to commit to {plan}, notice what you feel just before you answer, and whether "maybe" comes out first.
Next time you do commit to {plan}, notice how you feel in the day after: settled, or looking for a way out.
Next time a choice is small and easy to undo, like {choice}, notice whether you decide quickly.

pattern_types.name: Doing it all themselves rather than leaning on others
pattern_types.definition: When a job could be shared or help is on offer, the person does it themselves. Relying on others has let them down before, or they expect it to, so carrying it alone feels safer than waiting on someone who might not come through.
pattern_types.if_situation: A task could be shared or someone offers help
pattern_types.then_behaviour: Turns help down and does it all themselves
frameworks: Young's mistrust and emotional deprivation schema themes

signs.text: Turns down an offer of help on something that is clearly too much for one person
Says "it's quicker if I just do it myself"
Expects others to drop the ball, and names past times they did
Redoes work someone else already finished
Feels uneasy owing anyone a favour

signs_against.text: Hands over a part of something that matters and lets the other person do it their way
Does things alone because they enjoy it, and accepts help when it's needed

look_alikes.name: Saying yes and over-giving to feel needed
look_alikes.tells_apart: Keeps their own tasks so as not to depend on anyone; the other takes on other people's tasks to be needed

look_alikes.name: Saying "I'm fine" and hiding what's hard
look_alikes.tells_apart: Keeps their tasks to themselves so as not to be let down; the other keeps their troubles to themselves so as not to be a weight

look_alikes.name: Control-seeking under uncertainty
look_alikes.tells_apart: Distrusts people to come through, even when the outcome is clear; the other is uneasy about the outcome, whoever is doing it

pattern_types.anyone_would: Doing a task alone when nobody else is free or able to help

exclusions.text: Living alone through a crisis with nobody nearby to help

pattern_types.approved_wording: You seem to carry things yourself rather than lean on others, as if relying on someone is the bigger risk.
prediction_wordings: Next time someone offers to help with {task}, notice whether you say yes, and what you expect would happen if you did.
Next time you hand {task} to someone else, notice whether you check on it or redo part of it.
Next time you're stretched thin, notice whether asking {person} for help crosses your mind, and what you tell yourself about it.

pattern_types.name: Control-seeking under uncertainty
pattern_types.definition: When outcomes are uncertain, the person responds by planning, checking, gathering information or taking over. The discomfort comes from not knowing, and acting on it brings relief even when it changes nothing.
pattern_types.if_situation: An important outcome is unknown or depends on others
pattern_types.then_behaviour: Over-plans, seeks reassurance or takes control
pattern_types.function: To reduce the distress of uncertainty
frameworks: Big Five neuroticism (anxiety facet) with high conscientiousness

signs.text: Re-checks or refreshes for news on something they can't influence
Takes over a shared task rather than waiting on someone
Describes waiting as worse than a known bad outcome
Builds contingency plans for unlikely scenarios
Irritation when plans change at short notice, out of proportion to the cost

signs_against.text: Comfortably leaves an important outcome open for days
Plans heavily only where the stakes are concrete and planning changes the outcome (rational, not distress-driven)

look_alikes.name: Performance-contingent self-worth
look_alikes.tells_apart: Over-prepares because not knowing is the problem; the other over-prepares to prove their worth, and the unknown itself is bearable

look_alikes.name: Softening disagreement to protect belonging
look_alikes.tells_apart: Uneasy about any unknown outcome, closeness or not; the other keeps quiet only when closeness is at stake

look_alikes.name: Asking others to confirm a choice already made
look_alikes.tells_apart: Seeks information or control over an outcome still open; the other seeks agreement about a choice already made

look_alikes.name: Doing it all themselves rather than leaning on others
look_alikes.tells_apart: Uneasy about the outcome, whoever is doing it; the other distrusts people to come through, even when the outcome is clear

look_alikes.name: Reading silence as something wrong and reaching out to check
look_alikes.tells_apart: Uneasy about any unknown outcome; the other's not knowing is only about people and how they feel about them

pattern_types.anyone_would: A real crisis where control-seeking is adaptive

exclusions.text: Active health or safety emergency

pattern_types.approved_wording: Not knowing seems to weigh on you more than a bad answer would, so you reach for control.
prediction_wordings: Next time you're waiting on {outcome}, notice how often you check and what changes when you do.
Next time a plan changes at the last minute, like {plan}, notice what you do in the first few minutes.
Next time you get a clear answer on {outcome}, even a bad one, notice whether you feel calmer than you did while waiting.

pattern_types.name: Everything else goes quiet when something grabs them
pattern_types.definition: When a task, project or interest grabs them, the person goes all in and the rest of life drops away: meals, sleep, messages, plans. Being in the pull of it feels so good that stepping out feels like a loss.
pattern_types.then_behaviour: Goes all in and lets everything else drop
pattern_types.function: To stay in the pull of it
frameworks: Big Five openness and low orderliness

signs.text: Loses whole evenings or nights to one thing without noticing the time
Misses meals, sleep or plans because they were caught up in something
Leaves messages unanswered for days while on a project
Feels flat or irritable when made to stop
Moves from one all-consuming interest to the next

signs_against.text: Gets deeply into something and still stops for meals, sleep and people
Only goes all in near a real deadline, then goes back to normal

look_alikes.name: Healthy focus
look_alikes.tells_apart: Deep focus that they can step out of when life needs them, with nothing important dropped

look_alikes.name: Pulling back when someone gets closer or needs more
look_alikes.tells_apart: People drop away because something else has their attention; the other pulls away because the person is getting closer

pattern_types.anyone_would: Working long hours in the last days before a real deadline

exclusions.text: Using absorption to get through a loss or crisis

pattern_types.approved_wording: When something grabs you, everything else seems to go quiet, and coming back to the rest of life can feel like a loss.
prediction_wordings: Next time {interest} pulls you in, notice what you let drop, and how you feel when something makes you stop.
Next time you're deep in {interest}, notice the first thing that pulls you away, and how long it takes before you want to go back.
On a day when nothing has grabbed you, notice how the ordinary things feel, and whether you go looking for the next thing to fall into.

pattern_types.name: Moving the goal as soon as they reach it
pattern_types.definition: When the person reaches a goal, they barely pause before setting a bigger one. The win counts for little because the next target is already in view. Keeping a goal ahead means never having to ask whether they've done enough.
pattern_types.if_situation: Reaches a goal or gets a win
pattern_types.then_behaviour: Sets a new, bigger goal at once
pattern_types.function: So "enough" never has to be faced

signs.text: Talks about the next goal in the same breath as a win
Says reaching a goal "felt like nothing" or wore off in a day
Can't name a point at which they would be satisfied
Raises a target partway through because it now looks too easy
Skips or plays down marking a milestone

signs_against.text: Takes time to enjoy a win before thinking about what's next
Sets a new goal because they want it, not because the old one felt empty

look_alikes.name: Ambition with satisfaction
look_alikes.tells_apart: Aims higher after a win, but the win still felt good and counted

look_alikes.name: Performance-contingent self-worth
look_alikes.tells_apart: Moves the goal after succeeding; the other judges themselves after falling short

pattern_types.anyone_would: Setting the next step in a fixed path, such as the next exam in a course

exclusions.text: Money trouble that makes the next goal a real need

pattern_types.approved_wording: Each time you reach a goal, you seem to set the next one before the last one has had a chance to count.
prediction_wordings: When you next reach {goal}, notice how long you stay with it before your mind moves to what's next.
Next time someone congratulates you on {goal}, notice what you say back, and whether you mention what's still left to do.
Next time you finish something small, like {task}, notice whether it feels done, or whether a bigger version of it turns up at once.

pattern_types.name: Performance-contingent self-worth
pattern_types.definition: The person's sense of worth rises and falls with how well they perform. Falling short is felt as a verdict on the self, not on the work. High standards alone do not qualify; the marker is self-judgement after a miss.
pattern_types.if_situation: Performance is evaluated or falls short
pattern_types.then_behaviour: Self-criticism, over-preparation or putting the task off
pattern_types.function: To protect a sense of being worthy
frameworks: Self-critical vs high-standards dimensions of perfectionism (Frost and Hewitt–Flett traditions)

signs.text: Labels self after a mistake ("I'm useless") rather than the act
Discounts success as luck or as the minimum expected
Delays starting or shipping until it is "good enough"
Mood tracks recent output, e.g. a bad workday ruins the evening
Compares own output unfavourably with specific others

signs_against.text: Describes a failure with curiosity and no self-labelling
High standards that bring satisfaction, not dread

look_alikes.name: High standards (healthy)
look_alikes.tells_apart: A miss brings disappointment in the work, not in the self

look_alikes.name: Softening disagreement to protect belonging
look_alikes.tells_apart: Fears criticism as a verdict on their competence; the other keeps quiet to protect the relationship

look_alikes.name: Control-seeking under uncertainty
look_alikes.tells_apart: Over-prepares to prove their worth; the other over-prepares to reduce unknowns

look_alikes.name: Pushing back at once when criticised
look_alikes.tells_apart: Turns the criticism inward and judges themselves; the other turns it outward and answers back

look_alikes.name: Moving the goal as soon as they reach it
look_alikes.tells_apart: Judges themselves after falling short; the other moves the goal after succeeding

pattern_types.anyone_would: Disappointment after a real, costly setback, or preparing hard where the stakes are high

exclusions.text: Active burnout or job loss in the last month

pattern_types.approved_wording: How well you perform seems to decide how much you allow yourself to feel okay.
prediction_wordings: After the next piece of feedback on {domain}, notice whether your first thought is about the work or about you.
Next time you have {task} coming up that will be judged, notice how you get ready for it: more than it needs, or putting it off.
Next time something goes well in {domain}, notice how long the good feeling lasts, and what ends it.

pattern_types.name: Reading silence as something wrong and reaching out to check
pattern_types.definition: When someone close goes quiet, replies late or seems distant, the person reads it as a sign that something is wrong between them and reaches out to check. The checking is about the bond, and it settles them only once they hear things are okay.
pattern_types.if_situation: Someone close goes quiet or seems distant
pattern_types.then_behaviour: Reads it as trouble and reaches out to check
pattern_types.function: To feel secure in the bond
frameworks: Attachment theory, the closeness-seeking end (Bowlby; Fraley and Shaver)

signs.text: Sends a "are we okay?" or "did I do something?" message after a slow reply
Reads a short or late reply as a sign the other person is upset with them
Checks when someone was last online or re-reads past messages for clues
Can't settle until they've heard back
Sends a second message before the first has been answered

signs_against.text: Assumes a quiet partner or friend is just busy and carries on with their day
Checks in only after a real change, such as a missed plan or a row

look_alikes.name: Asking others to confirm a choice already made
look_alikes.tells_apart: Checks whether the bond is still okay; the other checks whether they chose right

look_alikes.name: Control-seeking under uncertainty
look_alikes.tells_apart: The not knowing is only about people and how they feel about them; the other is uneasy about any unknown outcome

look_alikes.name: Taking on other people's moods as theirs to fix
look_alikes.tells_apart: Reads distance as trouble for the bond and asks about it; the other reads a mood as theirs to fix and sets about fixing it

pattern_types.anyone_would: Checking on someone who has gone silent after saying they were travelling or unwell

exclusions.text: Any sign of abuse, threats or controlling behaviour in the relationship; that stays with the Safeguard
The other person really is in danger or missing

A long-distance relationship across time zones in its first weeks

pattern_types.approved_wording: When someone close goes quiet, you seem to read it as something wrong between you, and you need to check before you can settle.
prediction_wordings: Next time {person} takes a while to reply, notice what story you tell yourself about why, and what you do with it.
Next time you reach out to check on things with {person}, notice how long the relief lasts after they answer.
Next time someone you're less close to goes quiet, like {person}, notice whether you read anything into it.

pattern_types.name: Pulling back when someone gets closer or needs more
pattern_types.definition: When someone wants to get closer, asks for more time or leans on them, the person pulls back: slower replies, fewer plans, a sudden need for space. Closeness that grows feels like a claim on them, and stepping back keeps them their own.
pattern_types.if_situation: Someone gets closer or needs more of them
pattern_types.then_behaviour: Pulls back and makes more room
frameworks: Attachment theory, the self-reliant end (Bowlby; Fraley and Shaver)
Closeness and autonomy needs in couples (Baxter's dialectics)
Self-determination theory, autonomy need (Deci and Ryan)

signs.text: Wants more space soon after a relationship gets more serious
Feels crowded or smothered when someone asks to see them more
Goes cold on someone after a warm, close evening
Keeps parts of their life apart from a partner or close friend on purpose
Finds a fault in someone just as they start to like them

signs_against.text: Welcomes a partner or friend wanting more time together and makes room for it
Asks for space for a clear reason, such as a busy week, and comes back

look_alikes.name: Going quiet and pulling away when hurt
look_alikes.tells_apart: Pulls away when things get close, with no hurt before it; the other pulls away after being hurt

look_alikes.name: Keeping options open and putting off committing
look_alikes.tells_apart: Protects room from a person getting closer; the other protects freedom around choices and plans

look_alikes.name: Everything else goes quiet when something grabs them
look_alikes.tells_apart: Pulls away because the person is getting closer; the other lets people drop because something else has their attention

pattern_types.anyone_would: Keeping a stranger or new acquaintance who pushes for closeness at arm's length

exclusions.text: Any sign of abuse, threats or controlling behaviour in the relationship; that stays with the Safeguard
The other person is pushing past a no, or won't respect a limit
A breakup, separation or affair in the last month
Grief
Caring for a new baby, or a family member who is ill

pattern_types.approved_wording: When someone starts getting closer or needing more of you, you seem to step back to keep some room that's yours.
prediction_wordings: Next time {person} asks for more of your time, notice what you feel first, and whether you make a little more distance afterwards.
After your next long stretch of time with {person}, notice whether you want room to yourself, and how you go about getting it.
Next time {person} gives you space without being asked, notice whether you move a little closer.

pattern_types.name: Taking on other people's moods as theirs to fix
pattern_types.definition: When someone close is upset, tense or low, the person feels it as their own job to make it better, and steps in without being asked: cheering, smoothing, fixing. A calm mood around them is what lets them feel safe.
pattern_types.if_situation: Someone close is upset, tense or low
pattern_types.then_behaviour: Steps in to cheer, smooth or fix it, unasked
pattern_types.function: To keep things calm and feel safe

signs.text: Notices a shift in someone's mood straight away and can't relax until it lifts
Starts cheering up or sorting out a problem nobody asked them to sort
Asks "is it something I did?" when someone is in a bad mood
Changes their own plans to keep a tense person calm
Describes themselves as the peacekeeper in the family or group

signs_against.text: Lets someone be in a bad mood without stepping in, and stays at ease
Helps with a mood only when asked, and asks what would help first

look_alikes.name: Saying yes and over-giving to feel needed
look_alikes.tells_apart: Steps in to fix a mood without being asked; the other gives when asked

look_alikes.name: Softening disagreement to protect belonging
look_alikes.tells_apart: Acts to fix the other's mood; the other stays quiet about their own view

look_alikes.name: Reading silence as something wrong and reaching out to check
look_alikes.tells_apart: Reads a mood as theirs to fix and sets about fixing it; the other reads distance as trouble for the bond and asks about it

pattern_types.anyone_would: Comforting someone after a death or a real shock

exclusions.text: Any sign of abuse, threats or controlling behaviour; keeping someone calm may be about safety, and that stays with the Safeguard
Living with someone whose drinking, drug use or temper makes home unsafe
Caring for a family member with a serious illness
Grief in the family or friend group
Parenting a young child, where soothing moods is the job

pattern_types.approved_wording: When someone close is having a hard time, you seem to feel it's yours to fix, as if things aren't safe until they're calm again.
prediction_wordings: Next time {person} is in a low mood, notice how quickly you step in, and whether they asked you to.
Next time {person} is upset and you can't do anything about it, notice what that is like for you.
Next time the low mood belongs to someone you're not close to, like {person}, notice whether you feel the same pull to fix it.
